qs.q: A 54-year-old man with a growing mass lesion experiences a gradual rise in intracranial volume. Which mechanism acts as the initial compensatory response to buffer this volume change?
qs.e: The primary compensatory mechanism is the displacement of cerebrospinal fluid from the cranial vault into the spinal subarachnoid space. Vasoconstriction and parenchymal shifts occur later as capacity becomes exhausted.
qs.s: Cerebral Edema, Hydrocephalus, Raised ICP & Brain Herniation Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: Through which buffer system does blood maintain its stable pH range between 7.35 and 7.45?
qs.e: Blood maintains a stable pH range between 7.35 and 7.45 through buffer systems like carbonic acid. Fibrinogen is a plasma protein involved in blood clotting rather than acid-base regulation.

qs.q: Which chemical buffer system relies on the dissociation of imidazole groups?
qs.e: Hemoglobin acts as a buffer through the dissociation of its imidazole groups. Plasma proteins buffer via carboxyl or free amino groups, while the carbonic acid-bicarbonate system buffers via H2CO3 dissociation.
qs.s: Fluid and electrolyte balance disturbances: MCQs

qs.e: Ammonia buffers urine by combining with secreted hydrogen ions to form ammonium.

qs.q: Which buffer system is the PRIMARY extracellular buffer system in the human body?
qs.e: The bicarbonate-carbonic acid buffer system is the most important extracellular buffer system in the body. Its effectiveness stems from its high concentration and the fact that its components (CO2 and HCO3-) are readily regulated by the lungs and kidneys, respectively.

qs.q: Ammonia is an effective urinary buffer because ---
o: Its acid-base reaction has a low pKa
Kidney production decreases in chronic acidosis
qs.e: Ammonia acts as an effective urinary buffer because its pKa is favorable for trapping hydrogen ions.

qs.q: Ammonia is an effective and important urinary buffer for which of the following reasons
o: Renal tubule walls are impermeable to ammonia
Renal tubule walls are impermeable to ammonium
Its acid base reaction features a very low pKa
None of the listed choices are actually correct
Renal production decreases during chronic acidosis
qs.e: NH3 diffuses into tubular fluid where it combines with H+ to form NH4+. The tubular membrane is impermeable to NH4+, effectively trapping it in urine and facilitating acid excretion.

qs.q: Which buffer system is the PRIMARY extracellular buffer system in the body?
qs.e: ** The bicarbonate buffer system (H2CO3/HCO3-) is the primary extracellular buffer system, particularly in blood plasma, maintaining pH within the normal range of 7.35-7.45.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Buffers maintain pH by balancing weak acids and bases, crucial for enzyme activity and cellular function. Clinicians use buffer status to assess metabolic and respiratory disorders.

sections.p: Buffers are systems of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and conjugate acid) that resist pH change when acids or bases are added.
The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation relates pH to the ratio of conjugate base to acid. Small changes in H⁺ are absorbed by the buffer components.

t.b: Determines pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻ to identify respiratory vs metabolic disturbances; abnormal values indicate inadequate buffering.

sections.p: Homeostatic organs (lungs, kidneys, blood proteins) adjust buffer components. Respiratory compensation changes CO₂; renal compensation adjusts bicarbonate.
Impaired buffering leads to acid–base disorders. Causes include renal failure, severe diarrhea, sepsis, or toxin ingestion.
b: Metabolic acidosis: low HCO₃⁻, high anion gap; respiratory alkalosis: low PaCO₂

sections.p: Buffer status guides treatment: bicarbonate therapy, ventilation adjustments, or dialysis. Recognizing buffer failure prevents organ damage.
b: Severe acidosis can depress myocardial contractility and cause arrhythmias

t.b: Low indicates metabolic acidosis; high suggests metabolic alkalosis.
High suggests respiratory acidosis; low indicates respiratory alkalosis.

sections.p: Remember the three main buffer systems: bicarbonate, phosphate, hemoglobin. Use Henderson–Hasselbalch to calculate expected pH changes.
b: Bicarbonate buffer dominates in plasma; phosphate in intracellular fluids; hemoglobin in red cells.

faq.q: What is the most important buffer in blood?
faq.a: The bicarbonate–CO₂ system, because it accounts for ~70% of plasma buffering capacity.

faq.q: How does hemoglobin act as a buffer?
faq.a: Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds H⁺ released from CO₂ hydration, reducing pH change during tissue oxygen extraction (Haldane effect).
Yes, high intake of acidic foods can lower plasma bicarbonate, but the body compensates via renal excretion and respiratory adjustments.
